summary: This informational memo from AT&T/Neda specifies the Efficient Short Remote Operations protocol: its service model, notation and protocol, in version 1.2.

plainLanguage.summary: ESRO lets one program ask another program, somewhere else on the network, to do a small job and report back. It is built to add as little as possible to each message, because it was designed for wireless links. It works over UDP, so it has to cope with messages being lost.

questions: when should i use esro instead of rpc
how does esro save bandwidth on wireless
what is the difference between 2-way and 3-way handshake
subtitle: A lean remote procedure call protocol for short operations on unreliable networks.

tldr.problem: A remote procedure call over a wireless link has to work with very little overhead, and it cannot count on the network being reliable.
tldr.mechanism: ESRO runs on UDP and adds only a small header to each message. It offers two handshakes: a 3-way one where the invoker acknowledges the result, and a 2-way one where the result is confirmed by a timeout instead.
tldr.outcome: The protocol supports segmentation, reassembly and packing several messages into one datagram, and it identifies the encoding used for the parameters so that both ends agree. It has no authentication mechanism of its own.

today: RFC 2188 is an Informational memo from September 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The IESG note in the document records that the protocol had not had the benefit of IETF working group review and that a cursory examination revealed several issues which may be significant for scalability, so a site considering deployment is advised to conduct a careful analysis.

sections.title: Introduction and the Remote Operation Model
sections.content:
Efficient Short Remote Operations (ESRO) provide an efficient mechanism for the realization of Remote Procedure Call. This document specifies the service model, the notation and the protocol. The ESRO service is similar to and consistent with other Remote Procedure Call services, and the emphasis of both the service definition and the protocol is on efficiency. ESRO is designed specifically with wireless network usage, such as CDPD, in mind.

The protocol provides reliable connectionless remote operation services on top of UDP, or any other non-reliable connectionless transport service, with minimum overhead. It supports segmentation and reassembly, concatenation and separation, and multiplexing for service users, that is applications. ESRO allows trade-offs between efficiency and reliability by specifying both 2-way handshake and 3-way handshake based protocols. The encoding mechanisms for presenting the parameters of remote operations are outside the scope of the document, but identification, or tagging, of the encoding mechanism in use, such as XDR, BER or PER, is supported by the protocol. A variety of applications can use ESRO, and early users included efficient short message submission and delivery, credit card authorization and white pages lookup.

The overall model of ESRO is similar to and consistent with many existing protocols, and its distinguishing characteristic is efficiency. Remote Procedure Call defines a remote procedure model essentially the same as ESRO, but with a notation quite different from it, and RPC can rely on a connection oriented or a connectionless transport mechanism; when using the connectionless mechanism, retransmission and reliability issues are considered beyond the scope of the RPC specification. ROSE, the Remote Operation Service Elements, has a service definition similar to ESRO's and a similar notation, but the ESRO protocol itself is very different from the ROSE protocol. ESRO protocols can accomplish short operations with much less overhead than ROSE.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is deliberately small. Where a full remote procedure call carries a lot of machinery, ESRO carries just enough to make the call and report the outcome.

sections.title: ESRO Service Definitions
sections.content:
ESROS provides a service which supports interaction of applications based on a remote operation model. A remote operation is invoked by one entity; the other entity attempts to perform it and then reports the outcome. Users of ESROS assume the roles of invoker and performer. A user can assume both roles, being an invoker for some operations and a performer for others. The performer is expected to report either the result of the operation or an error: a result reply goes to the invoker if the operation succeeds, and an error reply if it does not. If the performer is unreachable, ESROS sends a failure indication to the invoker.

Operations are asynchronous, and the invoker may continue to invoke further operations without waiting for a reply. Synchronous or serialized operations are supported as a subset and a special case of the asynchronous service. By default the ESRO service provider on both the invoker and the performer sides supports the asynchronous operation invocation, but if one side is to support only the serialized, synchronous, mode, it should be in agreement with the peer side. ESROS has no authentication mechanism: authentication is the responsibility of the performer, which is outside the scope of ESROS, and the performer is not expected to honour the invoker when it is not authenticated.

The ESROS user reaches the services through an Efficient Short Remote Operations Service Access Point, the ESRO SAP. The RESULT, ERROR and FAILURE primitives can be implemented in two modes, an acknowledged result and a non-acknowledged result, and the difference between the modes is in their reliability of service and their efficiency. In the acknowledged result mode the result is acknowledged by the invoker, but the mechanism by which the acknowledgement is accomplished may not be reliable. The services are ESROS-INVOKE, which is non-confirmed, ESROS-INVOKE-P, which is provider-initiated, ESROS-RESULT and ESROS-ERROR, which may be confirmed or non-confirmed, and ESROS-FAILURE, which is provider initiated.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks, the other tries, and the answer comes back as a result, an error or a failure. The invoker does not have to wait for the answer before asking the next question.

sections.title: ESRO Service Notation
sections.content:
Users of ESRO services need to agree on a well defined set of parameters. They are the operation's argument data type, the operation's result data type, the operation's error data type, and the operation's value, a specific tag which uniquely identifies the operation. The invoker and the performer can specify these parameters using a variety of mechanisms; the notation specified in the memo is one such mechanism and is not the only one, since the ESRO protocol can be used independently of it.

The notation is defined by means of a macro facility, and it is very similar to the abstract operation defined in the ROSE documents, except that the value form of ES-OPERATION is always an integer. The ES-OPERATION macro gives a type notation of Argument, Result and Errors, and a value notation of a value with a local integer. The ERROR macro gives a type notation of Parameter and a value notation of a value with a local integer.

The mapping onto the services is direct. The invocation of an operation maps onto the ESRO-INVOKE service, the operation's value maps onto the Operation-value parameter, and the named type in the ARGUMENT clause maps onto the Argument parameter. A successful operation maps its reply onto the ESRO-RESULT service, with the named type in the RESULT clause mapped onto the Result parameter. An unsuccessful operation maps its reply onto the ESRO-ERROR service, with the value of the applied error mapped onto the Error parameter, and the named type in the PARAMETER clause of the ERROR macro of the applied error mapped onto the Error-parameter of that service.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the calls start, the two sides agree on what each operation is called and what shape its argument, its result and its errors have. The memo gives one way to write that agreement down.

sections.title: Protocol Overview, Service Access Points and Invoke IDs
sections.content:
The protocol realises the services defined earlier, and short operations are performed in a highly efficient manner. Two functional units are defined, which realise the services with 2-way and 3-way handshake, called the 2-Way Handshake Functional Unit and the 3-Way Handshake Functional Unit.

To access the ESRO services, an ESROS user binds to an ESRO Service Access Point and specifies whether the 3-Way or the 2-Way handshake functional unit is to be associated with it. The provider generates a SAP descriptor, which is passed to the user, and the handshaking for all Invoke requests addressed to that SAP, and for all PDUs addressed to it, follows the functional unit chosen at bind time. It is the responsibility of the two peer users to address their operations to the appropriate SAP, based on the agreement between them. An ESROS user starts the transfer of a PDU with the INVOKE service, and on receipt of an ESROS-INVOKE.request from the user the provider generates an Invoke ID and communicates it back to the invoker through the ESROS-INVOKE-P.confirm primitive.

The provider generates two invoke identifiers. The Invoke-Reference-Number uniquely identifies the invocation between the two peers, and is a PDU field 8 bits long. The Invoke-ID-Parameter uniquely identifies the invocation to the service user, and combines the Invoke-Reference-Number with the invoker address, the performer address and the SAP selector.

The Invoke-Reference-Number distinguishes several invocations in progress at the same time, which is what makes asynchronous operation possible, and it is also used as the segment identifier when a service data unit is transferred using segmentation and reassembly. The provider may reuse a reference number whenever it chooses, subject to the constraint that it may not reuse one that was previously assigned to an invocation for which it still expects, but has not yet received, a reply. The same value can be reused between different peer entities, because the combination of the peer address and the reference number still identifies the invocation uniquely.
sections.plainLanguage: Each call gets a number, so the answer can be matched to the question. The number is only eight bits, which is why it can be reused once the call is finished.

sections.title: Transfer, Handshakes and Segmentation
sections.content:
PDUs sent by UDP use port ESRO_CL_PORT, and PDUs carried by UDP are restricted to CLRO_SMALL_PDU_MAX_SIZE bytes. Each PDU is encapsulated in a single UDP datagram. For PDUs larger than CLRO_SMALL_PDU_MAX_SIZE but smaller than CLRO_SEGMENTED_PDU_MAX_SIZE, segmentation and reassembly are used, and each segment is transmitted in a UDP datagram. PDUs sent using UDP may be lost, and a retransmission strategy is defined; when a PDU is segmented, the strategy is not applied to individual segments, so the loss of one segment results in retransmission of the whole service data unit. The retransmission interval should be based on prior statistics if possible, since too aggressive retransmission can easily slow the response time of the network at large, and the minimum retransmission interval should be RETRANSMISSION_INTERVAL seconds. Delivery of PDUs is asynchronous, so ESROS does not wait for the result of a transmitted PDU and continues delivering the next PDUs.

The protocol is expressed as four separate transition diagrams, two for the invoker side and two for the performer side, one of each for the 2-way and the 3-way handshake. The 3-Way Handshake Functional Unit implements the acknowledged result model: the RESULT.confirm and ERROR.confirm primitives on the performer side are generated when an ESRO-ACK-PDU is received, and the failure indication on the performer side results from remote or local failures, so not receiving the ACK PDU or a local failure can produce it. The failure indication on the invoker side is generated if a local failure happens or an ESRO-FAILURE-PDU is received.

The 2-Way Handshake Functional Unit implements the not-acknowledged result model. The RESULT.confirm and ERROR.confirm primitives on the performer side are generated on a timeout, when no duplicate ESRO-INVOKE-PDU is received in a specified period of time. The failure indication on the performer side results from a local failure or after the retransmission timeout of the ESRO-RESULT-PDU or the ESRO-ERROR-PDU.

When a service data unit is too large to fit in a single connectionless PDU it is segmented and reassembled. The mechanism uses two additional PDU codes for a segmented INVOKE PDU, one byte of segmentation information holding a First/Other flag and a segment number, and the unused bits of the RESULT and ERROR PDUs to identify a segmented RESULT or ERROR PDU. All the segments in a sequence share the same Invoke-Reference-Number, the first segment specifies the total number of segments, and the others are numbered sequentially from 1. Each segment is transmitted in one UDP PDU, and the receiver should not impose any restriction on the order of arrival. A service data unit is not further processed unless all of its segments are received, and transmission of operation segments is not acknowledged, so the loss of one segment means retransmission of all of them. When acknowledged segments are wanted, the ESROS user should use the acknowledged result service instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The three-way version costs one extra message, the acknowledge, and in exchange the sender learns that the answer arrived. The two-way version saves that message and settles for a timeout.

sections.title: PDU Formats, Concatenation and Parameters
sections.content:
Five PDU types are used in the ESRO protocol, with the type coding set out in the memo: ESRO-INVOKE is 0, ESRO-RESULT is 1, ESRO-ERROR is 2, ESRO-ACK is 3, ESRO-FAILURE is 4, and ESRO-SEGMENTED-INVOKE is 5. The octets are numbered in increasing order starting from 1, and the bits of an octet are numbered from 1 to 8, where 1 is the low-order bit.

The ESRO-INVOKE-PDU format starts with the Performer SAP and four zero bits in octet 1, the Invoke Reference Number in octet 2, and in octet 3 a Parameter Encoding Type of four bits followed by an Operation Value of four bits, then the operation information in the remaining octets. The Invoker SAP is the Performer SAP minus one. The Parameter Encoding Type for an INVOKE PDU has the values 0 for BER, 1 for PER, 2 for XDR and 3 reserved. The Parameter Encoding Type for a RESULT PDU has the values 0 for Basic, 1 for Packed, 2 for XDR and 3 reserved.

Several ESRO-PDUs can be carried in one transport service data unit, using the ESRO-CONCATENATED-PDU, whose type code is 8. A concatenated PDU can contain one or more of the INVOKE, RESULT, ERROR, FAILURE and ACK PDUs, and the individual PDUs are distinguished by a one byte length indicator that comes before each of them. The number of PDUs in a concatenated PDU is bounded by the maximum length of the transport service data unit.

The protocol parameters are chosen to suit the subnetwork in use. CLRO_SMALL_PDU_MAX_SIZE should be chosen from the specifics of the subnetwork; in CDPD the maximum size of SN-Userdata can be up to 2048 bytes, and the optimum value may be smaller than the maximum the subnetwork supports. CLRO_SEGMENTED_PDU_MAX_SIZE and CLRO_MAX_PDU_SEGMENTS are chosen the same way, and in any case the last must be smaller than 127. The timers, that is the invoke PDU retransmission interval, the result and error PDU retransmission interval, the maximum number of retransmissions, the inactivity time and the reference number lifetime timer, are all to be specified and optimized for the network in use. ESRO uses UDP port number 259. The Security Considerations section says that ESROS has no authentication mechanism, and that authentication is the responsibility of the performer.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a few bytes: which kind it is, which call it belongs to, and which encoding was used for the data. Several messages can be packed into one datagram, with a length byte in front of each.

messages.label: ESRO-INVOKE-PDU
messages.note: Carries the operation, its arguments and the invoke reference number.

messages.label: ESRO-RESULT-PDU
messages.note: The operation succeeded; the result comes back.

messages.label: ESRO-ACK-PDU
messages.note: Confirms the result arrived, which is what the 2-way version leaves out.

items.label: ESRO-INVOKE
items.desc: The request that starts an operation.

items.label: ESRO-RESULT
items.desc: The successful outcome of an operation.

items.label: ESRO-ERROR
items.desc: The unsuccessful outcome of an operation.

items.label: ESRO-ACK
items.desc: The invoker's acknowledgement of a result or an error.

items.label: ESRO-FAILURE
items.desc: Tells the invoker that the performer could not be reached.

items.label: ESRO-SEGMENTED-INVOKE
items.desc: One segment of a large invoke.
